solutions.check: grid and clues read from the FT's printable PDF, its numbering matching the clue list; every fifteensquared answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Theatre is heaving after introduction of superb harmonica player

indicators.note: after tells us the heaving part comes behind the opening letter and the player
the introduction of a word is its opening letter, here taken from superb

parts.note: Larry Adler was a famous harmonica virtuoso
the sea that is heaving swells

explanation.surface: A London theatre is buzzing after a top harmonica player opens the show.
explanation.walkthrough: SADLER'S WELLS is a London theatre famous for dance; Larry Adler was the best-known harmonica player of the twentieth century.
explanation.definitionFit: Sadler's Wells is a celebrated London venue for dance and opera, so it is a theatre by name.

clue.text: Like a clergyman in pantomime?

parts.note: a la, borrowed from French, means in the style of or like
DD, Doctor of Divinity, is a title held by clergymen
taken as written

explanation.surface: Is the vicar dressing up for the Christmas show?
explanation.walkthrough: The 'a' joins the pieces; pantomime is the British Christmas stage show for families, and ALADDIN is one of its stock stories.
explanation.definitionFit: Aladdin is one of the traditional stories staged as a British Christmas pantomime, so it names one by example.

clue.text: Old jockey wins in Irish town

indicators.note: wins is read as gains or takes in, so the jockey's name takes the next word inside it

parts.note: Lester Piggott was a famous English jockey of the past
taken as written

explanation.surface: A retired jockey takes victory in a race in an Irish town.
explanation.walkthrough: Lester Piggott was Britain's most famous flat-racing jockey; 'wins' is read as takes in, signalling a container.
explanation.definitionFit: Leinster is strictly the eastern Irish province around Dublin, so the setter's town is a loose description of an Irish place name.

clue.text: Relative overseas principally tracks Gaelic man?

indicators.note: principally means taking the principal, first, letter of each of the two words

parts.note: RY is short for railway, a set of tracks

explanation.surface: A relative abroad mostly follows a Gaelic man's trail.
explanation.definitionFit: Rory is a common Irish and Scottish Gaelic given name, so the question mark marks a man named by example.

clue.text: Royal canine puts female servant outside, spilling one salad ingredient?

indicators.note: the servant is put outside, so her letters wrap round the royal and canine pieces
spilling means losing, so a letter is dropped from the servant

parts.note: a waitress is a woman serving at table
one is the Roman numeral I
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the royal cipher
C is the dental shorthand for a canine tooth

explanation.surface: A royal dog makes a waitress take the blame for spilling a salad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spilling one' drops I from the servant to give WATRESS, which then wraps round the royal and canine letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Watercress is a peppery leaf eaten raw, a common salad green, hence the example question mark.

clue.text: Run out of extra stout? Light beer needed

indicators.note: out of means the run letter is taken away from the larger word

parts.note: something extra stout is larger
R is the cricket abbreviation for a run

explanation.surface: With the stout gone, a drinker settles for a lighter beer.
explanation.definitionFit: Lager is a pale, light-bodied beer, the usual contrast to a dark stout.

clue.text: Northern clan come from opposite directions in the beginning

indicators.note: in tells us the directions sit inside the beginning

parts.note: the beginning is the start
E and W, east and west, are opposite compass points

explanation.surface: A Highland clan gathers from all sides at the outset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'come from' only links; the Stewarts are a Scottish clan, hence northern.
explanation.definitionFit: The Stewarts are a Scottish clan, the royal house of Scotland, and Scotland lies in the north of Britain.

clue.text: Suggest what a balloon might do?

definitions.meaning: to put forward an idea tentatively, as if letting it drift for others to consider
literally, a balloon drifts aloft above the ground

explanation.definitionFit: To leave an idea hovering is to suggest it tentatively, and literally a balloon drifts above the ground.

clue.text: British seaside town, one neglected in wild shantyman tales

indicators.note: wild means unruly, so the remaining letters are rearranged
neglected in means a letter within the phrase is left out

parts.note: A is the indefinite article, meaning one

explanation.surface: A sailor's yarns run wild in a British resort.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop one A from SHANTYMAN TALES and rearrange the rest. LYTHAM ST ANNES is a resort on the Lancashire coast, near Blackpool.
explanation.definitionFit: Lytham St Annes is a resort town on the Lancashire coast of England, so it is a British seaside town by name.

clue.text: Educational department that is, in France, more green

parts.note: LEA is a Local Education Authority, a British education department

indicators.note: in tells us the that-is letters go inside the France abbreviation

parts.note: ie, id est, means that is

explanation.surface: An education office in France grows greener.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in France' looks like a French translation clue; in fact FR (France) holds IE (that is).
explanation.definitionFit: Something leafier has more foliage and so looks more green, a comparative adjective in both cases.

clue.text: Passed over food in party dress

indicators.note: in tells us the food goes inside the party

parts.note: the Tory party is the British Conservatives

indicators.note: passed over is read as flipped over, so the food is turned backwards

parts.note: an egg is a food

explanation.surface: Someone skipped the buffet at a party in their best clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Toggery is old slang for clothes or garments, so it means dress in the sense of attire.

clue.text: Ignoring cold, precariously ascend these?

indicators.note: precariously suggests something unsteady, so the remaining letters are rearranged
ignoring means leaving out the cold letter

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold on a tap

explanation.surface: Climbers scale these peaks unsteadily, shrugging off the cold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ignoring cold' removes C from ASCEND; the rest is shuffled. The whole clue also hints at climbing a range.
explanation.definitionFit: The Andes are a high South American mountain range that climbers ascend in the cold, which the whole clue describes.

clue.text: New bar manager's final promise — a centre for smokers?

indicators.note: new suggests a fresh arrangement of the letters of bar
the final letter of manager's

parts.note: an oath is a solemn promise

explanation.surface: A new pub landlord vows to make the place friendly to smokers.
explanation.walkthrough: ARBROATH is a Scottish fishing town famous for the Arbroath smokie, a smoked haddock, so the smokers are fish, not people.
explanation.definitionFit: Arbroath, on the Scottish coast, is where the smoked haddock called smokies are made, hence a centre for smokers.

clue.text: Work up sprint on river where one hears bass?

parts.note: OP is short for opus, a work

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the sprint word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: to hare is to run fast, to sprint
the Ouse is an English river

explanation.surface: A worker sprints up by the river where the fish lurk.
explanation.walkthrough: Bass looks like the fish beside the river; here it is the low singing voice heard in an opera house.
explanation.definitionFit: An opera house is a theatre where audiences hear singers, among them bass voices.

clue.text: They entertain spy back in private quarter

indicators.note: in tells us the reversed spy word goes inside private

parts.note: inner means private, as inner thoughts

indicators.note: back means the spy word is read backwards

parts.note: to peek is to spy
S, south, is one of the four quarters of the compass

explanation.surface: Agents hide a spy in a secret part of town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns the spy word to give KEEP; the quarter is a compass point.
explanation.definitionFit: Innkeepers host and look after guests, so they entertain them in the hospitality sense.

clue.text: Hole in the wall contains old fragment

indicators.note: contains tells us the cash machine holds the old letter

parts.note: hole in the wall is British slang for a cash machine, an ATM

explanation.surface: A gap in an old wall hides a fragment of the past.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hole in the wall' looks like a gap in masonry; it is British slang for a cash machine, ATM.
explanation.definitionFit: An atom is a tiny particle or speck, so it can mean a fragment of something.

clue.text: Photograph centre of Venice in party, backtracking — it's a difficult thing

indicators.note: in tells us the photograph and the centre sit inside the party
backtracking means the party word is read in reverse

parts.note: Con is short for the Conservative party
a pic is a photograph

indicators.note: the centre of Venice is its middle two letters

explanation.surface: A snapshot of Venice at a party that goes into reverse proves awkward.
explanation.walkthrough: CON reversed gives NOC, which holds PIC and NI (the middle of Venice).
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom no picnic describes something hard or unpleasant, the opposite of an easy outing.

clue.text: Latest ones in that taxi quaffed whisky neat

indicators.note: the latest ones are the last letters of each of the following words

explanation.surface: In the taxi, someone downed a whisky without water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'neat' looks like it describes the whisky, unmixed; it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Tidy and neat are synonyms, both meaning orderly and well kept.

clue.text: Domestic furnishing — a clothes-horse?

definitions.meaning: a kitchen sideboard with shelves for plates
a person who wears clothes, playfully a stylish one

explanation.definitionFit: A dresser is a sideboard for crockery, and also, whimsically, someone who dresses, like a fashion-conscious clothes-horse.

clue.text: Accommodation between seaman and militants upset toff

indicators.note: upset means overturned, so the whole string is read backwards
between tells us the cots sit between the seaman and the militants

parts.note: a tar is a sailor
cots provide sleeping accommodation
the IRA is the Irish Republican Army, a militant group

explanation.surface: Militants and a sailor fight over lodgings, upsetting a posh gent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns the whole string round at once; a toff is British slang for an upper-class person.
explanation.definitionFit: Toff is British slang for a wealthy or upper-class person, a near synonym of nobleman.

clue.text: Umpire complimentary about Essex's opener, following on

indicators.note: following tells us the complimentary part comes after the on part

parts.note: re means on or concerning

indicators.note: about tells us the free word goes round the opener

parts.note: complimentary means free of charge

indicators.note: the opener of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: An umpire gets a free pass at Essex's opening match.
explanation.walkthrough: The free word goes about E to give FEREE. Essex is an English county with a cricket team.
explanation.definitionFit: Referee and umpire are both officials who enforce the rules in a game.

clue.text: Sense agreement among crew

indicators.note: among tells us agreement goes inside the crew

parts.note: an eight is a rowing crew of eight oarsmen
yes is a word of agreement

explanation.surface: The crew come to an agreement about something sensible.
explanation.definitionFit: Eyesight, the faculty of vision, is one of the five senses.

clue.text: Poem wicked, crossing boundaries of decency

indicators.note: crossing means the wicked word straddles the boundary letters

parts.note: ill can mean wicked, as ill deeds

indicators.note: the boundaries of a word are its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A poem so wicked it oversteps the bounds of decency.
explanation.definitionFit: An idyll is a short pastoral poem describing rural life.

clue.text: Female you texted in pub for a laugh

indicators.note: in tells us the female and you letters go inside the pub

parts.note: an inn is a pub
in text-message shorthand you is written U

explanation.surface: A woman texts you from the pub just for a laugh.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase in fun means jokingly, done for a laugh rather than seriously.

clue.text: Pork pie husband has once?

parts.note: a pork pie is a type of hat with a flat crown

explanation.surface: A husband eats a pork pie, or did once.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pork pie' looks like the British meat pastry; it is a flat-crowned hat. 'Once' marks the definition as old usage.
explanation.definitionFit: Hath is the archaic third-person form of the verb have, so it meant has in older English.

clue.text: A TV company restricted by evidence of debt? Would you believe it!

indicators.note: restricted by means held in, so the TV company sits inside the debt note

parts.note: an IOU is a written note acknowledging a debt
Sky is a British television company

explanation.surface: A TV company is hemmed in by its debts, to everyone's disbelief.
explanation.definitionFit: The exclamation I ask you expresses exasperated disbelief, like Would you believe it!

clue.text: Race venue isn't always given backing

parts.note: ain't is a colloquial form of isn't

indicators.note: given backing means the always word is put in reverse

parts.note: e'er is a poetic contraction of ever, always

explanation.surface: A racecourse that does not always get financial support.
explanation.walkthrough: 'given backing' sounds like betting support at the races; it reverses EER. AINTREE, near Liverpool, hosts the Grand National.
explanation.definitionFit: Aintree is the racecourse near Liverpool that hosts the Grand National, so it is a race venue.

clue.text: Limousine this Roman takes before important game

parts.note: a Roller is slang for a Rolls-Royce, a luxury limousine
hoc is Latin for this, as a Roman would say it
key means important, as a key point

explanation.surface: This Roman takes a limousine to a big match.
explanation.definitionFit: Roller hockey is a team sport played on roller skates, so it is a game.
